text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Kellogg v. Rouches,

2013 BCSC 946

Date: 20130530

Docket:
13 0927

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Vivian
P. Kellogg

Plaintiff

And

Inga
Kellogg Rouches, Executrix of the Will

of Robert P. Kellogg, Inga Kellogg Rouches, Executrix

of the Will of Lisa E. Kellogg, Inga Kellogg Rouches,

Successor
trustee of the Kellogg Family trust, and

Susanna M. Kellogg

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Abrioux

Reasons for Judgment

The Plaintiff, Vivian Kellogg:

appearing
in person

Counsel for Defendant, Inga Rouches:

Heather
Fisher

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

April

May

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,

I:          INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The defendant Inga Kellogg Rouche, executrix of
the will of Robert P. Kellogg, applies to have the notice of civil claim struck
on the ground that it discloses no reasonable claim. In the alternative, she
seeks to have the notice of civil claim struck on the ground it is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or an abuse of the process of the Court.
She also seeks special costs against the plaintiff.

[
2
]

The plaintiff applies to have the defendant
added as a defendant in her personal capacity and is seeking costs.

[
3
]

As at the date of the hearing of this
application the defendant, Susanna Kellogg, had been served with the notice of
civil claim. She resides in the United States of America and the time limit for
her filing a response had not yet elapsed.

[
4
]

The plaintiff is acting on her own behalf.
Following the hearing of this application on April 23, 2013, I granted her
leave to file supplementary written submissions. That occurred on May 3, 2013.
The defendant’s reply was filed on May 8, 2013.

[
5
]

The defendant takes issue with much of the plaintiff’s
submissions on the basis that many of the allegations of fact are not before
the Court either by way of affidavit evidence or as presently pleaded in the notice
of civil claim.

[
6
]

This application is brought pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a)
of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
. Rule 9-5(2) provides that no evidence
is admissible on an application under subrule (1)(a). I have applied this
subrule in my review of the materials filed or relied on by the plaintiff.

[
7
]

For the reasons that follow, I have concluded
the notice of civil claim should be struck on the ground that it discloses no
reasonable claim. In the alternative, it should be struck on the grounds it is
frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of the Court’s process.

II:         BACKGROUND

[
8
]

The pertinent background facts are summarized in
the defendant’s submissions:

3.         Robert
P. Kellogg died on April 15, 1999, leaving a last will and testament, dated March
23, 1994 (the “Will”). The testator was survived by his wife, Lisa, and his three
daughters, the Plaintiff, Vivian P. Kellogg, and the Defendants, Inga Kellogg
Rouches, and Susanna M. Kellogg;

4.         The
Will appointed Lisa as the “personal representative” and the Defendant, Inga
Kellogg Rouches as the alternate “personal representative”;

5.         At
the time of the testator’s death, he owned an interest in real property located
on Salt Spring Island, B.C.;

6.         Lisa
died in 2010 without having obtained a Grant of Probate of the Will and without
having dealt with the testator’s interest in the real property;

7.         The
Defendant, Inga Kellogg Rouches, applied for a Grant of Probate, which was
opposed by the Plaintiff, on the grounds that the Will was not valid because it
was procured by fraud and undue influence;

8.         On
October 30, 2012, this Honourable Court pronounced the Will in solemn form (the
“Proof in Solemn Form Order”);

9.         On
November 28, 2012, this Honourable Court granted letters probate of the Will to
the Defendant, Inga Kellogg Rouches;

10.       On
November 28, 2012, the Plaintiff filed a Notice of Appeal of the Proof in
Solemn Form Order, whereby she seeks to set aside the Order. The Plaintiff has
not yet filed a Factum, and her grounds for appeal are not known;

11.       The
Plaintiff filed her Notice of Civil Claim on March 12, 2013. She alleges that
the Defendant is not entitled to act as Executor of the Will, and has obtained
the grant of probate and appointment as Executor, through misrepresentation of
material facts and fraud on the Court.

III:        THE
PLAINTIFF’S CLAIMS AND THE BASIS FOR THE DEFENDANT’S APPLICATION

[
9
]

The issues raised in the plaintiff’s claim as
set out in the notice of civil claim appear to be twofold in nature:

(a) should the
defendant have been appointed as executor of her father’s will after her mother
Lisa Kellogg (as the first named executor) purportedly acted and served as executor
without having obtained a grant of probate? To put the issue another way,
should an administrator of the will have been appointed?

(b) did the
defendant withhold information from the Probate Registry and/or make
misrepresentations to the Court and, on that basis, should the grant of  probate
be revoked?

[
10
]

The notice of civil claim refers to
“misrepresentations”. The principal allegation is referred to in paragraphs 48
to 54 of the notice of civil claim. It appears to relate to a document filed
with the Probate Registry on November 22, 2012. It contained a statement to the
effect that “Lisa E. Kellogg predeceased the Testator…”

[
11
]

This statement was clearly in error. The notice
of civil claim, however, recognizes that the error was known as at the time the
grant of probate was issued on November 28, 2012. That is because the Grant
itself states:

Be it known that Lisa E. Kellogg died
after

the said testator, without having obtained probate of the said Will.

[Emphasis added.]

[
12
]

The notice of civil claim in paragraph 8 of Part
1 specifically refers  to fraud:

The Plaintiff
seeks revocation of the grant of probate on the grounds that the Defendant Inga
K. Rouches, “Executrix of the Will of Robert P. Kellogg”, is not entitled to
act as an Executor of the Will, and has obtained the grant of probate and
appointment as Executor, through misrepresentation of material facts and fraud
on the Court.

[
13
]

Particulars are then set out in paragraphs 9 to
54 of the notice of civil claim.

[
14
]

At paragraphs 10 and 11 of her written
submissions, the plaintiff states:

The basis I am seeking revocation of the
grant of probate after proof of the Will in solemn form, is on the grounds of
fraud. This fraud, is “fraud on the court”.

Fraud on the
Court is a part of what will be raised in my appeal.

[
15
]

In her submissions, the plaintiff alleges that
the information withheld by the defendant from the Court prior to the grant of
probate was:

(a) her mother,
Lisa Kellogg acted as executrix after her father’s death; and

(b) information
pertaining to a trust was also withheld.

[
16
]

The plaintiff’s written submissions are to the
effect that since Lisa Kellogg in fact acted as executrix, Mr. Kellogg’s
property could not vest in the defendant as at the time of Mr. Kellogg’s death.
Furthermore, the information about the trust being withheld from the Court affects
the appointment of the executor because, amongst other reasons:

•

the defendant may not have the authority to deal
with the assets;

•

the will does not dispose of property other than
through the trust;

•

if the trust were not incorporated into the will,
the defendant would be in a conflict as both a successor trustee and executor
of the will;

•

the nature of the trust changed after Lisa
Kellogg’s death;

•

the property could not vest in Lisa Kellogg from
the date of Mr. Kellogg’s death and at the same time be said to vest in the
alternate executor and successor trustee as at the date of Mr. Kellogg’s death.

[
17
]

The defendant’s position on this application can
be summarized as follows:

(a) the facts
pleaded by the plaintiff do not disclose any misrepresentation of material
facts or fraud on the part of the defendant that would disentitle her from
acting as executor;

(b) the basis of
the plaintiff’s claim is confusing and it is difficult to understand what the
plaintiff takes issue with;

(c) proof of the
will in solemn form provides protection for the will. It will not later be set
aside unless obtained by fraud or a later will is found;

(d) the plaintiff
has not pleaded that the defendant fraudulently obtained the proof in  solemn
form order;

(e) revoking the grant
of probate will not result in the will being found invalid, thereby creating an
intestacy. This will only arise if the order for proof in solemn form is
revoked. To revoke that order, the plaintiff must claim and prove that it was
obtained by fraud;

(f) the proof in
the solemn form order is under appeal;

(g) the plaintiff
claims she is entitled to revocation of the grant of letters probate given her
intestate interest in her father’s estate. She has no standing to bring this
action given that what she is seeking by way of the notice of civil claim will
not result in an intestacy;

(h) the plaintiff’s
notice of civil claim does not set out any material facts which support even
prima
facie
evidence of fraud.

[
18
]

In addition, the defendant notes that in
paragraph 16 of her written submissions, the plaintiff states that on April 23,
2012, [
sic
2013] she filed a petition with the Court seeking directions
as to whether the gift to the trust can occur and whether the trust may be
incorporated by reference into the will.

IV:       THE APPLICABLE PRINCIPLES

[
19
]

The principles that apply to this application
are the same as those that applied under the predecessor rule, being R. 19(24).
They can be summarized as follows:

(a) the question
as to whether a pleading discloses no reasonable claim is to be determined on
the basis that the facts as pleaded are true. Where it is “plain and obvious”
that the claims as pleaded or, as amended, would disclose no reasonable claim,
the Court has the discretion to dismiss it. Any doubt is to be resolved in
favor of allowing the pleadings to stand.

Hunt v. Carey
Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at 980;
Citizens
of Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C.
(4th) 266 at para.
34
(B.C.S.C.).

(b) irrelevancy
and embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it
is difficult to understand what is being pleaded… “A pleading is ‘frivolous’ if
it is obviously unsustainable...”

Citizens of
Foreign Aid Reform
at para. 47.

(c) a pleading is
frivolous if it is without substance, is groundless, fanciful, “trifles with
the court” or wastes time;

Borsato v.
Basra
,
2000 BCSC 28
at para.
24
.

(d) furthermore,
it is vexatious if it is without a
bona fides
, is “hopelessly
oppressive” or causes the other party anxiety, trouble or expense;

Borsato
at para.
25
.

(e) a  pleading,
to avoid being embarrassing, must not be concealing or evasive. It must state
the real issue in an intelligible form.

Borsato
at para.
26
.

(f) abuse of
process is a flexible doctrine that allows the Court to prevent a claim from
proceeding where it violates such principles as “judicial economy, consistency,
finality and the integrity of the administration of justice”.

Toronto
(City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63

at para.
37
.

(g) categories of
abuse of process include those that “involve a deception on the court or
constitute a mere sham; where the process of the court is not being fairly or
honestly used, or is employed for some ulterior or improper purpose;
proceedings which are without foundation or serve no useful purpose and
multiple or successive pleadings which cause or are likely to cause vexation or
oppression.”

Babavic v.
Babowech
,
[1993] B.C.J. No. 1802 at para. 18
(S.C.)
.

V:        DISCUSSION

[
20
]

When I examine the allegations set out in the notice
of civil claim within the context of the legal principles to which I have
referred, I conclude the notice of civil claim offends Rule 9-5 (1) (a), (b)
and (d) and should be struck. That is because:

(a) it does not
establish a cause of action. The plaintiff does not appear to appreciate the
difference between probate of a will on the one hand, and its construction on
the other. Whether the trust document has been incorporated by reference into
the will is not specifically pleaded. In any event, this is an issue of
construction and the will cannot be construed in the absence of probate;

(b) in addition, the
plaintiff in April 2013  filed a petition with the Court whereby she is seeking
the proper construction of the will and directions as to whether the gift to
the trust can occur and whether the trust may be incorporated by reference into
the will;

(c) the plaintiff
alleges fraud and yet fails to plead any material facts to support that
allegation;

(d) the plaintiff
alleges misrepresentations were made to the Probate Registry and yet the notice
of civil claim sets out that the Registry was aware of the alleged misrepresentation
as at the time probate was granted;

(e) the plaintiff
was unsuccessful in the action that resulted in the proof in solemn form order
being made on October 30, 2012. In my view, what is being sought by the
plaintiff in this action is an attempt to do indirectly what she was unable to
do directly in that proceeding. The fact the plaintiff commenced further
proceedings in April 2013, relating to the construction of the will, is a
further indication that this action is an abuse of process;

(f) paragraph 2 of
the notice of civil claim alleges that the plaintiff is entitled to a share of
her father’s estate “in the event of an intestacy”. What the plaintiff seeks in
this action, being a revocation of the grant of probate, will not result in the
will being found invalid and a resulting intestacy. The will has been proved in
solemn form in BC Supreme Court, Victoria Registry action number 12-1843. The
plaintiff has filed a notice of appeal in relation to the proof of solemn form
order.

[
21
]

There is also no basis set out in the notice of
civil claim for an order of costs including special costs against Mr. Horne.

[
22
]

In her written submissions, the plaintiff makes
reference to certain alleged representations of Mr. Horne, which “may have been
a factor in the defendant concealing information”. In addition, it is said that
Mr. Horne’s actions have had “at a minimum, a financially detrimental impact
[on] all parties with an interest in my father’s estate”.

[
23
]

The plaintiff also points to the fact Mr. Horne
has not provided an explanation for submitting the letter referred to in
paragraphs 51-52 of the notice of civil claim six days after the date of the grant
of probate.

[
24
]

In her oral submissions, the plaintiff stated she
was proceeding under the assumption that the defendant did ”whatever Mr. Horne
asked her to do” and that Mr. Horne had an obligation to provide the Court
what was needed.

[
25
]

As I will refer to below, a claim for special
costs is based on either egregious conduct or conduct “worthy of reproof or
rebuke”.

[
26
]

Even if I were to assume the allegations
contained in the plaintiff’s written submissions were contained in the notice
of civil claim, they would not provide the basis for an order of costs, let
alone special costs against Mr. Horne. There are simply no material facts pleaded
in the notice of civil claim or contained in the submissions that  could provide
the basis for such an award, if the notice of civil claim was amended.

VI:       COSTS

[
27
]

The defendant seeks special costs on the basis
the plaintiff’s conduct is “deserving of reproof or rebuke”:
Garcia v. Crestbrook
Forest Industries Ltd.
(1994),
1994 CanLII 2570 (BC CA)
, 9 B.C.L.R. (3d) 242 para.
17
(C.A.).

[
28
]

The defendant submits the plaintiff’s conduct
includes:

•

in the proof in solemn form action, the
plaintiff alleged the will was invalid on the basis of fraud and undue
influence. She presented no evidence to substantiate these allegations. She was
unsuccessful and has filed a notice of appeal. She then commenced this action
seeking a revocation of the grant of probate. Once again she alleges fraud with
the allegation not being supported by a plea of any material facts;

•

the action had no reasonable prospect of
success. While this is not in itself a basis for awarding special costs, when
combined with improper allegations of fraud, it may become sufficiently
reprehensible to warrant such an award. (
Garcia
at para.
23
);

•

this action amounts to harassment of the
defendant. The plaintiff has taken unreasonable, illogical and unsubstantiated
positions. The defendant as  executor has a duty to defend the will. The estate
continues to incur expenses as a result of the plaintiff’s actions.

[
29
]

The defendant seeks $4,000 in lump sum special
costs, payable forthwith. She submits this is a reasonable amount taking into
account the time spent defending the action, including the hearing of this
application, and the additional expense incurred in reviewing the plaintiff’s
written submissions and replying to them.

[
30
]

The plaintiff has not responded to the
defendant’s submissions with respect to special costs.

[
31
]

In my view, an award of special costs is
appropriate in this case. The plaintiff has chosen to persevere in her
allegations of fraud and misconduct notwithstanding the result in the prior
Supreme Court action. She has done so without making any plea of material facts
that would,
prima facie
, support such a serious allegation.

[
32
]

In addition, for the reasons outlined above, I
view this action to amount to an abuse of process. The plaintiff’s conduct is
causing the estate to incur significant expenses.

[
33
]

I am satisfied  the plaintiff’s conduct is
deserving of reproof or rebuke. In my view the sum of $3,500, inclusive of
taxes and disbursements, is appropriate. I award special costs in that amount.

VII:      CONCLUSION

[
34
]

The notice of civil claim is struck and the
action is dismissed. The plaintiff is ordered to pay the defendant $3,500 in special
costs inclusive of taxes and disbursements.

[
35
]

Since the notice of civil claim is struck, I
need not deal with the plaintiff’s application to add the defendant in her
personal capacity as a party to the proceeding.

“Abrioux
J.”
